baseline_incident_edges.relationship: argues for women’s historical agency and supports documentary recovery
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. The complete 1946 preface supplies the attributed agency argument; Voss-Hubbard reconstructs collaborative archival practice and its institutional/racial limits. Neither proves universal emancipation or sole founding.
baseline_incident_edges.map_label: Agency, records and contested archival practice

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: invites comparison between earlier agency-centered history and later recovery groupings
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: An editorial test of Hunt’s grouping, not a claim that Beard adopted the later language of identity politics. Beard questions the historical subject-sex premise and equality as a sufficient guide in her preface. This remains a comparison with later identity questions, not their origin or a shared unified position.
baseline_incident_edges.map_label: Historical agency and the category of women

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Schwimmer and Grierson help shape archival projects through proposal, disagreement and sustained institutional work
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Voss-Hubbard pp. 19–30 differentiates Schwimmer’s pacifist project from the broader WCWA and Grierson’s collecting/access work at Smith. Collective practice is not doctrinal agreement or sole authorship.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Black women’s archival participation exposes unequal authority and support within WCWA
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Voss-Hubbard pp. 20–21 reports Thurman/Bethune/NCNW involvement and dissatisfaction, with no Black directors and limited support for fieldwork. This criticism of organizational practice is mediated through the 1995 study, not a claim that all Black women shared one response or a direct refutation of the 1946 book.
baseline_incident_edges.map_label: WCWA: racial inclusion, authority and resources

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Mary Beard coauthors broad histories of American civilization with Charles Beard
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The Rise of American Civilization (1927) and America in Midpassage (1939) are documented collaborative works. Precise division of authorship and identical interpretations are not established; her separate women’s-history work remains distinct.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Charles Beard participates in the documented partnership of historical writing
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The reciprocal contribution names a particular coauthor rather than a uniform school acting on Mary Beard. No surviving correspondence between the couple is claimed, nor a precise allocation of chapters.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Recovers Beard’s historical work through a selected edition of her letters, editorial commentary and an introductory assessment.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Cott’s own1991 preface explains selection, commentary and documentary treatment, including omitted late letters attacking Charles Beard’s critics and the role of the literary heirs. Her introduction treats Mary as a historian in her own right. This is scholarly editorial recovery, not evidence that Mary formally mentored Cott. The full correspondence remains unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Questions Beard’s treatment of the conflict between domestic responsibilities and women’s opportunities in public life.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: In the selected1991 introduction paragraph beginning She considered, Cott appreciates Beard’s radical challenge to private/public divisions but observes that she looked away from conflicting domestic and public demands. Cott finds her civilizing-power account more comfortable and persuasive for societies with less elaborated public/private divisions. This particular reservation accompanies substantive recovery and praise; it does not reject Beard’s whole work. The source jumps from the displayed48 archive passage to this domesticity paragraph without a connecting page header; its original printed page is uncertain. The next sentence is cut off and supplies no claim.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Davis’s comparative biographies develop through women’s-history teaching, source discovery and revised questions of significance
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Davis names the 1971 course with Conway and Colie’s Glikl suggestion in her acknowledgments. Her prologue and conclusion compare three lives while retaining religious difference and colonial power. This primary selection supplements the existing catalogue description; it is not a full source audit or a claim that women’s history originated biography.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Davis, Conway and Colie: teaching into research

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Beard connects political institutions to economic interests
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Applies to the Progressive side of this paired node, not to all consensus history; economic interpretation does not by itself establish Marxist affiliation. Preface and chapter XI opening supply Beard’s own framing; his constitutional data and inferred motives have not been replicated.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: invites comparison of materialist explanation with Beard’s economic interpretation
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: No Marxist identity or simple derivation is attributed to Beard, and no common economic method to consensus historians.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: intersects in Becker’s and Beard’s arguments about interpretation and objectivity
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Benson explicitly challenges the economic-determinist interpretation he attributes to Turner and Beard
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Chapter VIII opening names both historians. The target is the Progressive side of the paired entry and a specified interpretation; it is not criticism of every argument by them or every consensus historian.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Benson: criticism of economic-determinist voting history

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Beard cites Cunningham on testing historical hypotheses
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Chapter 1 invokes William Cunningham’s methodological advice. This specific citation does not establish agreement on all economic interpretations.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Libby’s sectional mapping supplies Beard with a resource
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Beard’s preface and chapter 1 explicitly credit Libby; the latter’s introduction explains the procedure and its proxies.
Chapter 1 criticizes a named national-history account while recognizing documentary scholarship. Beard’s characterization is a polemic, not an exhaustive description of Bancroft.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Hartz disputes Marx’s explanation of socialist ideology
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Chapter 1 section 2 proposes an alternative relation between feudal heritage and socialist thought. This is Hartz’s claim alone; the existing Beard/materialism comparison remains distinct.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Bederman cites Lears’s account of neurasthenia among the resources for explaining anxieties about allegedly depleted white middle-class male vitality.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Body14/n54 uses No Place of Grace (1981),49–57 with Gosling, the jointly authored Haller study, Rotundo and Lutz, alongside contemporary George Beard. This is a specific plural resource, not an exclusive origin for the book’s argument or an endorsement of the historical disease categories. The Lears original remains unread.
